To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

patients with comorbid major depressive disorder (MDD) and anxiety disorders show increased resting-state functional connectivity of the limbic and the salience network with regions in the precuneus, lingual gyruses, posterior cingulate gyrus, precentral gyrus and middle frontal gyruses.

comorbid patients with depression and anxiety showed an increase in functional connectivity of a limbic network with the bilateral precuneal cortex, intracalcalarine cortex, lingual and posterior cingulated cortex, and the right precentral, inferior and middle frontal gyri.
comorbid depression-anxiety patients show increased limbic network functional connectivity, which was not found for patients with either depression or anxiety alone.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the investigation of resting state functional connectivity (RS-FC) of the brain in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD), patients with anxiety disorders (AN), and patients with both disorders (COM).
the investigation of the neural mechanisms underlying comorbidity of depression and anxiety.
the investigation of resting state networks in patients with depression, comorbid anxiety and anxiety disorders.

the comorbidity of depression and anxiety is not associated with abnormal resting-state functional connectivity of the limbic, default-mode, salience, or sensory-motor networks.

the limbic network is altered in patients with comorbid depression-anxiety, but not in patients with depression or anxiety disorders only.
the limbic network is involved in comorbid depression/anxiety, but not in either depression or anxiety alone.
